title: What connects a community?

sections.label: What to keep
sections.title: Keep these three points.
items: One newsroom reaches the people it already serves. Two newsrooms that ask one question reach more of them.
A shared question needs one editor who holds the schedule and one place to put the work.
Every number in this sample is invented. Replace each one with a result you can source.

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: This page is the sample report of the CCM report template. It shows each part of a report in the order a reader meets it: the points to keep, the argument, a stage that changes as you scroll, a figure, a table, the results, a chronology, the terms, the method and the sources. The subject is invented. Use the page to judge the shape of a report, not the evidence in it.

sections.label: The question
sections.title: A story is only the beginning.
paragraphs: A reporter asks a question. A resident shares what they know. An editor connects the account to a wider story. Each exchange gives information a place to go.

A newsroom that works alone answers the question for its own readers. A newsroom that shares the question answers it for a region. That is {collaborative reporting}, and it is the subject of this sample.[^1]

paragraphs.pullquote: A newsroom that shares the question answers it for a region.

paragraphs: This sample follows a small set of imagined newsrooms. Scroll to see the drawing change with the story. The marks are a picture of an idea. They do not measure reach.
notes: Invented example. The drawing holds the same twelve marks in every layout. The count is a decision about the picture, not a result.

sections.label: Follow the connections
sections.title: From one newsroom to a shared network.

steps.title: Start with the people doing the work.
steps.text: Each mark stands for one imagined newsroom. At first, the marks sit apart. Each newsroom has its own sources, routines, and readers.
steps.caption: 12 imagined newsrooms, working independently

steps.title: Make room for a shared question.
steps.text: A common reporting question brings newsrooms into small groups. Partners can compare records, share translation, and identify gaps in coverage.
steps.caption: Three groups, each convened by one newsroom

steps.title: Build connections that last.
steps.text: As partners exchange work, individual projects can become a network. The lines show possible relationships, not measured information flows.
steps.caption: A connected network of 12 imagined newsrooms

steps.title: Keep the community at the center.
steps.text: The shared work matters when people can find and use it. A report should explain who benefits, what changes, and what the evidence cannot tell us.
steps.caption: Shared work returns to a common public purpose

sections.label: What comes next
sections.title: Leave the reader with a clear next step.
paragraphs: Explain what the results mean for the people who can act on them. Connect each recommendation to evidence in the report, and say who has to do the work.

A group that shares a question can also share the parts that cost the most. A {shared beat} spreads the cost of one reporter. A {news commons} gives the group one place to plan. An agreement for {content sharing} puts the finished work in front of more readers.
Use the method note to say how you gathered the evidence. Name the limits, so a reader can judge what the report supports and what it does not.

terms.definition: Two or more newsrooms that report one story together. Each one publishes the work in its own voice.
One reporter who covers a subject for several newsrooms at once. The newsrooms share the cost and publish the same reporting.
A network that gives the newsrooms of one region a place to plan, to train and to share what they make.
An agreement that lets a partner republish another partner's story, with credit, at no cost.

sections.text: A useful report lets the reader see the evidence, follow the reasoning, and ask a better question.
